Prompt: Use the uploaded character reference image as the strict identity and outfit reference.

Preserve the reference character’s:
- face identity
- facial proportions
- eye shape
- nose
- lips
- skin tone
- hairstyle
- hair color
- visible hair accessories
- overall recognizable vibe
- outfit and styling shown in the reference image

Do not hardcode any specific character traits that are not present in the uploaded reference.
All identity, hairstyle, accessories, and clothing details must be inferred directly from the uploaded reference image.

Create a high-quality mixed-style vertical portrait showing:
1. a realistic full-body version of the uploaded character/person
2. a black hand-drawn doodle-shadow version of the same character/person on the wall beside them

Core concept:
The real person and their doodle-shadow are doing a playful mischievous pose together.
The real person performs a cute realistic version of the pose, while the doodle-shadow performs a much more exaggerated, chaotic, cartoonish version of the same pose idea.
The mood should feel cute, playful, mischievous, stylish, funny, and social-media-friendly.

Real person:
- Must remain realistic and photogenic
- Must wear the same outfit style and key visible details from the uploaded reference image
- Do not replace the reference styling with unrelated fashion
- Expression should be cute, slightly confused, mildly embarrassed, playful, as if thinking: “Why am I doing this with my shadow?”
- The real person should not stand stiffly
- The real person should actively participate in the pose, but in a natural realistic way

Doodle-shadow:
- Must be a black hand-drawn sketch version of the same person, drawn directly on the wall
- Not a realistic second person
- Not a normal physical shadow
- Not a full-color anime character
- Black sketch line-art only
- Should resemble the person through hairstyle silhouette, accessories, outfit silhouette, and pose structure
- The doodle-shadow should look more energetic, sillier, and more chaotic than the real person
- Add manga-like motion lines, hearts, stars, sparkles, and comic marks around the doodle if helpful

Random mischievous pose rule:
The pose must NOT be fixed.

For each generation, invent a new playful mischievous pose for both the real person and the doodle-shadow.
The real person and the doodle-shadow should share the same general pose idea, but they do not need to match perfectly.
The real person performs a cute realistic version.
The doodle-shadow performs a much more exaggerated, chaotic, cartoonish version.

Do not repeatedly use pointing poses.
Do not repeatedly use finger-gun poses.
Do not repeatedly use the same standing pose.
Do not always make both figures simply point at each other.

Create a different mischievous pose each time.

Possible pose directions are loose inspiration only, not a fixed menu:
- playful idol pose
- silly dance pose
- leaning sideways with one arm curved overhead
- making a big heart pose
- cheeky wink pose
- hands near cheeks in a cute teasing pose
- exaggerated “ta-da!” pose
- mock surprise pose
- playful running-in-place pose
- mischievous tiptoe pose
- arms stretched in opposite directions
- pretending to sneak away
- cute troublemaker pose
- dramatic overreaction pose
- goofy victory pose
- playful balance pose
- playful peekaboo pose
- shy but mischievous pose
- cute overconfident pose

The final pose should feel fresh, cute, mischievous, and slightly chaotic.
The real person should look like they are reluctantly playing along.
The doodle-shadow should look like it is having way too much fun.

Composition:
- vertical 4:5 or 9:16
- show the real person in full-body or nearly full-body framing
- place the real person on one side of the frame
- place the black doodle-shadow on a clean wall beside them
- the doodle-shadow should be roughly the same height or slightly taller
- keep enough space around both figures so the full pose is visible
- the connection between the real person and the doodle-shadow must be clear at a glance

Background:
- simple clean indoor studio wall or minimal room corner
- white, cream, or pale gray wall
- clean floor
- soft natural sunlight patch or gentle wall shadow allowed
- keep the background uncluttered

Lighting:
- soft natural studio lighting
- bright, clean, polished, playful mood
- keep the real person’s face clearly visible

Style quality:
- realistic human photography
- black hand-drawn doodle-shadow on wall
- matching mischievous pose interaction
- strong identity resemblance
- outfit and styling faithfully based on the uploaded reference
- cute and stylish mixed-media portrait
- clean composition
- social-media-friendly
- no obvious AI artifacts

Negative prompt:
hardcoded blue hair when not in reference, hardcoded cloud clip when not in reference, hardcoded fish clip when not in reference, hardcoded school uniform when not in reference, outfit change unrelated to reference, realistic second person, normal reflection, normal shadow only, solid black monster shadow, horror shadow, creepy shadow, full-color illustration, cartoon human, anime human, weak resemblance, unrelated sketch character, messy wall, cluttered background, repeated pointing pose, repeated finger-gun pose, same pose every time, fixed pose, boring mirrored pose, stiff pose, identical pose repetition, real person not matching shadow pose, text, watermark, logo, distorted body, extra limbs, extra fingers, bad hands

An Olin College undergraduate dropped out of school in 2014 to run a machine learning company out of his dorm room. He had no PhD, no plans to get one, and no interest in a public research career.

Two years later he joined OpenAI as a research scientist. Over the following eight years he wrote or co-wrote the papers that introduced GPT-1, GPT-2, CLIP, DALL-E, and Whisper, work that has now been cited more than 190,000 times.

Sam Altman would later call him a genius at the level of Einstein. Deep learning pioneer Jeff Clune would call him the father of modern generative AI. He has not posted on social media since May 2021.

His name is Alec Radford.

Here is the story, because the person who quietly wrote the foundational papers of modern AI did it without a graduate degree, without a research team of his own, and without a public profile.

Alec grew up in the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs of Texas. He built his first computer at the age of five with help from his father. He graduated from Cistercian Preparatory School in 2011 as an Eagle Scout, then enrolled at Franklin W. Olin College of Engineering, a small private school in Massachusetts known for its very low acceptance rate and its project-based curriculum.

He never finished the degree. In 2013 he and three classmates, Slater Victoroff, Diana Yuan, and Madison May, founded a machine learning company called indico out of their dorm room. Luke Metz joined the team the following year. The startup was accepted into Techstars Boston in the summer of 2014 and raised a $3 million seed round by the end of that year. Alec dropped out of Olin in August 2014 to run research at the company full time.

While there, in November 2015, he co-authored DCGAN with Luke Metz and Soumith Chintala. The paper introduced the first generative adversarial network architecture that trained reliably at scale, and it set the template for generative image research for years. He was twenty-two years old.

He joined OpenAI as a research scientist in 2016. His first project was an attempt to train a language model on around 2 billion Reddit comments. It failed. His response was to try again with a different dataset. In 2017 he trained a multiplicative LSTM with 4,096 units on 82 million Amazon product reviews. Training took a full month on four NVIDIA Pascal GPUs. The model was only supposed to predict the next character. What it did instead was learn a single neuron that tracked the sentiment of the text on its own, without ever being told what sentiment was. The paper, co-authored with Rafal Jozefowicz and Ilya Sutskever, was called "Learning to Generate Reviews and Discovering Sentiment." It was one of the first clear pieces of evidence that scale alone could produce structured internal representations, and it changed how Ilya thought about the future of language modeling.

In June 2018 Alec was the first author on a short paper called "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training." It introduced GPT-1, a 117 million parameter Transformer trained on unlabeled text. The paper is modest and almost apologetic in tone. It is also the seed of every frontier model that exists today.

In February 2019 he was the lead author on GPT-2, a 1.5 billion parameter version of the same idea. OpenAI initially declined to release the full weights, citing concerns about misuse, and the resulting news cycle put the lab on the map of the general public for the first time.

In January 2021 he was the primary author on CLIP, which trained an image encoder and a text encoder against 400 million image-text pairs collected from the internet. The model made multimodal AI tractable and became the visual grounding layer for the entire text-to-image generation wave that followed. He co-authored the DALL-E paper the same month.

In September 2022 he was the lead author on Whisper, a 680,000 hour speech recognition model that flattened the commercial speech industry with a single research release.

Through all of it he did not lead a team in the executive sense. He was a technical individual contributor who kept picking the right experiment, running it cleanly, and writing it up without hedging. Many of the notebooks that produced these results were initially built in Jupyter. He posted his last tweet in May 2021 and largely disappeared from public view.

In December 2024 Alec told colleagues he was leaving OpenAI to do independent research. By April 2025 he had surfaced as an advisor at Thinking Machines Lab, the startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati with much of the lab's senior research bench.

A researcher without a PhD, without a team, and without a public profile spent nine years quietly writing the canonical papers of modern AI.

He did it by picking the right experiment and shipping it, over and over, without waiting for anyone to notice.

🤖 Significant AI Breakthroughs That Changed the World

♟️ 1997 — Deep Blue
A computer defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, showing that machines could outperform elite humans in tightly defined intellectual tasks.
🧠 2012 — Deep Learning Breakthrough
AlexNet dramatically improved image recognition and helped trigger the modern deep-learning era.

🎯 2016 — AlphaGo
AlphaGo defeated Go champion Lee Sedol, demonstrating advanced pattern recognition, planning, and reinforcement learning in a game once considered beyond machines.
🔤 2017 — The Transformer
The Transformer architecture made it far easier to train powerful language models and became the foundation of much of today’s generative AI.

🧬 2020–2021 — AlphaFold 2
AI began predicting protein structures with accuracy often competitive with experimental methods, transforming structural biology and biomedical research.
💬 2022 — Conversational Generative AI
ChatGPT brought large language models into everyday public use, allowing millions of people to interact with AI through natural conversation.

🎨 2022–2023 — Multimodal Generation
AI systems rapidly improved at generating and interpreting text, images, audio, video, and computer code.
🧪 2024 — AlphaFold 3
AI expanded beyond individual proteins to predict interactions involving proteins, DNA, RNA, small molecules, and other biological components.

papers i keep telling people to read if they want to actually understand modern AI:

1. Attention Is All You Need by @NoamShazeer et al (the transformer)
2. FlashAttention by @tri_dao (why training actually got fast)
3. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models by @hojonathanho (diffusion, before it was cool)
4. Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning by @_jasonwei (reasoning just appears at scale)
5. LoRA by @edwardjhu (fine-tune anything on one GPU)
6. Mamba by @_albertgu & @tri_dao (attention isn't the only way)
7. Direct Preference Optimization by @chelseabfinn et al (RLHF, minus the RL)

save this list

Machine verifiable reward is a proxy for "useful to a human" and a model optimises the proxy it is handed rather than the one you meant. So this is not an alignment failure but it is alignment doing exactly what you specified, toward a cheaper target.

Human preference is costly to measure but checkable correctness is nearly free and optimization drains toward whatever is cheapest to score.
